meta.title: Who really said "We do not see things as they are, we see them as we are"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Anaïs Nin did write the line — but as a quotation, crediting "talmudic words." Quote Investigator finds no true origin: the saying is anonymous.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We do not see things as they are, we see them as we are'?
meta.ogDescription: Nin quoted it, she didn't coin it — and the Talmud passage everyone cites is about dreams. Variants run back to 1831. Origin: anonymous.

answer.label: Not Anaïs Nin — she was quoting an older saying
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · in English print by 1831 · quoted by Anaïs Nin, 1961
answer.sourceLine: The words really do appear in Anaïs Nin’s novel Seduction of the Minotaur (1961) — but not as her own. She writes them as a quotation: “Lillian was reminded of the talmudic words.” Nin credited the line to someone else, and Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that its true origin is unknown and the saying should be labelled anonymous.
answer.confidenceText: The wording is genuine to Nin’s book; the authorship credit is not.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: 1961, Swallow Press — the final volume of Nin’s Cities of the Interior sequence; an earlier version appeared in 1958 as Solar Barque
Quoted by Nin, not coined by her — she attributes it to the Talmud

source.excerpt: Lillian was reminded of the talmudic words: “We do not see things as they are, we see them as we are.”
trail: 1801 & 1831 — the idea is already in English print. Quote Investigator ↗ documents a Sydney Smith sermon of 1801 warning that we judge “not as the truth of things is, but as we are ourselves,” and a piece titled “Things As They Are” in The Atlas of 1 May 1831: “We cannot see things as they are, for we are compelled by a necessity of nature to see things as we are.” Both predate Nin by well over a century.

1961 — Nin quotes it, and says so. Seduction of the Minotaur, page 124, carries the modern wording verbatim — introduced as “the talmudic words.” Wikiquote ↗ lists the saying under its Disputed section, citing this novel.

The Talmud check fails. The passage usually offered as the source is Berakhot 55b. Read it: Sefaria ↗ gives Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani on dreams — “A person is shown in his dream only the thoughts of his heart.” That is a claim about dreaming, not about perception, and the modern formulation is not there.

The verdict. Quote Investigator’s conclusion is blunt: the saying has been used by Nin, H. M. Tomlinson and Stephen Covey among others, “however, its origin is not known, and it is not possible to provide a precise ascription. Hence, the expression should be labeled anonymous.”
source.excerptNote: Note the framing. Nin sets the line inside quotation marks and hands the credit away in the same breath. Every version of this quote that ends “— Anaïs Nin” is quoting a woman who was herself quoting, and who told you so.

source.rightsNote: No public-domain claim can honestly be made here, because the line has no established origin to date — Quote Investigator labels it anonymous. Separately, the specific text we excerpt above, Nin’s 1961 novel, is itself firmly in copyright: the Internet Archive ↗ holds its Swallow Press printing as a lending-restricted scan, not a free download.

author.name: Anaïs Nin
author.kicker: The writer who gets the credit
author.heading: Anaïs Nin — the messenger, not the source
author.bio: Born Angela Anaïs Juana Antolina Rosa Edelmira Nin y Culmell in Neuilly-sur-Seine, Nin kept a diary prolifically from the age of eleven until her death, and it is the diaries — not the novels — that made her name. She also wrote fiction and became one of the best-known writers of female erotica of her century. Seduction of the Minotaur (1961), the closing volume of her Cities of the Interior sequence, is where the famous line surfaces — and Nin, to her credit, never claimed it. She wrote it as a quotation and pointed elsewhere. The internet removed the quotation marks.

copyAttribution: "We do not see things as they are, we see them as we are." — Anonymous, not Anaïs Nin. Nin quoted the line in Seduction of the Minotaur (1961), crediting it to "talmudic words" — but Berakhot 55b is about dreams, and Quote Investigator finds variants back to 1831 with no known author. Via quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Three credits, none of which hold
misattribution.intro: This is an unusually layered case. The quote is not fabricated, and it is not absent from Nin’s work — it is right there on page 124. What’s wrong is the arrow: the credit points at the person who was passing the line along, and then at a source she named but never verified.

items.why: Her novel contains the exact wording, which is why the attribution is so sticky — but she presents it as a quotation and assigns it to the Talmud in the same sentence. Wikiquote ↗ accordingly files it under Disputed rather than among her sourced lines.

Once Nin called it “talmudic,” the saying was widely re-credited to the Talmud with no version or passage cited. When a passage finally was named, it didn’t match: Berakhot 55b ↗ says a person is shown in a dream only the thoughts of his own heart — dream interpretation, not a theory of perception. Quote Investigator finds the assignment to the Talmud lacks strong support.

Henrik Scharling’s Nicolai’s Marriage credited the statement to Kant in 1876, and the Kant version still circulates. Quote Investigator ↗ reports it has not located the line anywhere in Kant’s writings.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who said it first. The thought was circulating in English by 1801, had reached near-final shape in The Atlas by 1831, and passed through H. M. Tomlinson in 1931 and Stephen Covey’s 7 Habits before and after Nin carried it into 1961 — and Quote Investigator ↗ concludes it “should be labeled anonymous.”

context.heading: Why this one spread so well
lead: Most fake quotes fail a simple test: the words aren’t in the author’s books. This one passes that test and is still misattributed, which is what makes it interesting. A reader who checks page 124 of Seduction of the Minotaur finds the sentence exactly as advertised, closes the book satisfied, and never notices that Nin wrote the words with quotation marks around them.

The line also had two things going for it: an aphorism short enough to survive any retelling, and a first-person plural that flatters the reader into the insight. Attach a bohemian diarist’s name and it becomes shareable; attach the Talmud’s and it becomes ancient wisdom. Neither credit was ever checked, because a quote this satisfying doesn’t feel like it needs checking.
context.detailsSummary: The variants, and the writers who also passed it along
detailsBody: The saying’s survival is a good illustration of how attribution drifts upward toward famous names. The 1831 Atlas version — “We cannot see things as they are, for we are compelled by a necessity of nature to see things as we are” — is wordier and anonymous, so it died. The compressed 1961 version had a name attached, so it lived.

It is worth noting that H. M. Tomlinson used a variant in his 1931 collection Out of Soundings (“We see things not as they are, but as we are ourselves”) and Stephen Covey later carried another into The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (“We see the world, not as it is, but as we are”). None of these writers coined it either. They were all doing what Nin did: passing along a good line that already had no owner.
context.pull: Nin put the line in quotation marks. The internet took them out.
